 How to fund Australia’s future
by Erin-Lea Brown, Matthew Bowes
 21.10.2026 
 Podcast
 Share 
 Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.com Bluesky 
 Australia’s budgets are under pressure. Debt is rising, interest bills are climbing, and the costs of an ageing population and climate change are still ahead. So how did we get here? And what would it take to fix it?
 The biggest challenges now sit in state budgets, and the GST is no longer doing the job it was designed to do.
 In this podcast, Grattan Economic Prosperity Deputy Program Director Erin-Lea Brown talks to Senior Associate Matthew Bowes about our report, Budget reboot: How to fund Australia’s future, which sets out a plan to repair budgets through stronger fiscal rules, a bigger and broader GST, and a new deal between federal and state governments.
 Grattan Institute · Economy: How to fund Australia's future 
 Transcript
 Erin-Lea Brown: Budget pressure is rising across Australia’s federation. Both the federal government and the state governments are staring down escalating debt, and rising interest rates will add billions more to the bill. We are moving into a harder and more expensive world, and the demands on state and federal governments keep increasing.
 This matters because of the known risks ahead. From an ageing population and the growing costs of climate change, to rising demand for health and disability services, all of these pressures will require governments to have the fiscal firepower to act.
 So how did Australia get here, and what would it take to fix it?
 That’s the focus of Grattan’s new report, Budget reboot: How to fund Australia’s future .
 Welcome to The Grattan Podcast. This podcast is being produced on the lands of the Wurundjeri people. Grattan acknowledges and celebrates the First Nations people on whose traditional lands we meet and work, and whose cultures are among the oldest in human history.
 I’m Erin-Lea Brown, Deputy Program Director of our Economic Prosperity Program. Today I’m joined by my co-author on the report, Matthew Bowes, Senior Associate in the program. Matt, welcome.
 Matthew Bowes: Thanks so much for having me, Erin.
 Erin-Lea Brown: I wanted to start by asking you: if you had to use three words to describe Australia’s budget position right now, what would they be?
 Matthew Bowes: I’d have to say health, infrastructure, and interest costs. They’re the three biggest cost pressures that states are facing. What would your three words be?
 Erin-Lea Brown: My first word is tight. Budgets are tight. The environment around them is tense. And my final word is trade-offs. How we manage all of this really comes down to trade-offs.
 Matthew Bowes: Tight, tense, and trade-offs. That’s a tricky combination.
 Before we get into the detail of the report, it might be useful to set some context for listeners. Grattan has been calling for budget repair and GST reform for many years. So why this report now, and how much more urgent has this problem become?
 Erin-Lea Brown: We’re in a period of change and uncertainty. The world is less stable, and when it comes to future crises, it’s really a matter of when, not if.
 But our budgets are brittle. The era of cheap borrowing is over, and long-term pressures are continuing to build at the same time: ageing, growing demand for health and care services, climate change, and slower economic growth.
 All of this makes the task of balancing the budget fundamentally harder, and governments are meeting this new environment with very little room to move. The problems have also shifted to the budgets of Australia’s states, which are responsible for delivering the core services we rely on.
 Grattan’s earlier work focused on federal budgets, particularly after the global financial crisis and COVID. But since the pandemic, the states have driven the rise in national debt – that’s state and federal debt combined. The states’ share of national debt is forecast to almost double, from 20 per cent before the pandemic to about 38 per cent by 2030.
 For the most part, states are expected to stay in deficit. Deficits are forecast to continue in most states over the next four years, with only the NT forecasting falling gross debt as a share of its economy next year. Budget repair is still a choice today, but the longer we wait, the fewer choices we’ll have.
 And at this particular moment, the federation’s funding is actually up for debate. The Productivity Commission’s 2026 inquiry into how the GST is shared between the states has opened a window for rethinking how we fund the states.
 Matthew Bowes: That sounds right to me. It’s the right time for a conversation about budget deficits and how we can fix them.
 Erin-Lea Brown: Matt, I mentioned that state budgets are where the biggest fiscal challenges currently are. It’s worth noting that when we talk about state budgets in this context, we mean all of Australia’s states and territories.
 So what is the state of state budgets across Australia? How bad is it?
 Matthew Bowes: It’s pretty problematic, Erin. Part of the challenge is that the weakening in state budgets happened gradually and then all of a sudden. Over the last 20 years, state operating expenses grew by 13 per cent as a share of the economy, while revenue grew by just 5 per cent.
 That means more of the gap is being filled by borrowing and by the federal government. The pandemic steepened that climb in spending, while revenue just hasn’t kept up.
 Not every state is in the same position, and that’s relevant to this conversation. Western Australia and Queensland have big mining sectors. New South Wales and Victoria are the largest economies with the largest share of the population, while states like Tasmania have older and smaller populations. All of that affects the budget challenges and spending needs they face.
 But when we looked across the budgets of the eight states and territories, we found a range of shared challenges. The biggest is demand for health services that just keeps growing. Health is the fastest-growing area of state spending. It’s risen by about 1.2 per cent of GDP since 2003, which is more than the combined increase in all other areas of government expenditure.
 Voters also now expect governments to help them through crises and cost-of-living shocks, not just in Australia but across advanced economies. We can see the spending pressures, and the pressure for tax cuts, that this creates in the state election cycle in places like Victoria and New South Wales.
 Pandemic-era commitments are also still flowing through, particularly in state infrastructure programs. States announced a robust set of capital investments to support the post-COVID recovery, but they’ve since run into supply chain problems and cost escalation, and that’s caused budget blowouts. State capital spending has averaged 2.1 per cent of GDP over the last five years, up from just 1.4 per cent in the five years to 2010. That increased infrastructure spending is a significant driver of state deficits.
 Other pressures include rising wage costs, with some states lifting or scrapping public sector wage caps from 2022.
 And of course, borrowing is just more expensive. States now need ever-larger savings just to stop interest costs adding to debt, before they even start to close the structural deficit. In 2026, states are budgeted to spend almost $21 billion on interest on government debt. That’s more than the $17 billion they spend on housing, community amenities, and environmental protection combined.
 To put that in perspective: in 2019, at interest rates as they were then, every $1 billion in deficits that state governments ran up cost $180 million in interest payments over a decade. At today’s interest rates, that same $1 billion in deficits costs $760 million over a decade. That’s more than a fourfold increase, and it just adds to the challenges state budgets face.
 Erin-Lea Brown: When you set out all of the challenges like that, you really see what a remarkable set of circumstances we find ourselves in. Listening to it, I also wonder how we can possibly get back to delivering recurrent surpluses. It seems really tough.
 Matthew Bowes: It does seem really tough. All states have taken at least some steps to get their budgets back on track since the pandemic, but those efforts don’t seem to match the size of the problem. I know you’ve worked in a couple of state treasuries, so I’d be interested to hear why you think it’s so difficult for states to bring spending and revenue back into balance.
 Erin-Lea Brown: Having worked inside state treasuries and for state governments, I know that no one sets out to run up a bunch of debt. There are really smart people working in these organisations, both officials and ministers, and they’re working hard to get good outcomes.
 But they’re balancing really tricky trade-offs. So we wanted to understand why, despite real effort, the numbers keep moving the wrong way. We looked at about 15 years of state budgets, comparing what governments planned to spend with what they actually spent, and we saw the same patterns showing up across the country, despite the differences you outlined, Matt.
 The first thing we found is that states have what we call a soft budgeting problem. They set budgets assuming they’ll keep costs down more than they realistically can. When the budget’s blown, the government tops it up, then sets another tight target, and around the cycle goes again. We’ve seen this play out for about 15 years in health, social protection, and public order, but particularly in health.
 Another pattern is in how states forecast their revenue. Some of their big revenue sources, like stamp duty and mining royalties, jump around a lot, so they’re hard to predict. Our analysis suggests treasuries manage that uncertainty by forecasting them cautiously, and on average, revenue tends to come in higher than treasuries expect.
 That should be good news. But our analysis finds that this surprise revenue tends to get used to cover overspends or fund new programs, rather than repay debt. And once that money’s spent, it’s very hard to get it back out of the budget base. A new program or a bigger hospital budget becomes part of the government’s base funding, and the harder it is to control costs in an area, the more windfalls get soaked up this way.
 Matthew Bowes: And it’s not necessarily a problem that governments are conservative in how they forecast revenue. That’s probably a good thing when you’ve got really hard-to-predict revenue sources. The challenge is that it’s not actually constraining spending. Governments still expect the windfall to come through, and they use it to fund additional spending rather than seeing it for what it is: a variable source of revenue that might fall in future and that they can’t bank on to fund ongoing expenses.
 Erin-Lea Brown: That’s exactly right. And so the report recommends stronger fiscal rules, and independent budget offices in every state, as part of the solution.
 Matt, how does Grattan propose these institutions be designed? How would they constrain governments without preventing them from responding to genuine shocks?
 Matthew Bowes: We found that almost every state currently has a fiscal strategy, and the targets in those strategies often look really good on paper. They’re laudable in targeting debt reduction and deficit repair.
 But ultimately, those targets aren’t strong enough to guide budget decisions. They’re often vague, without specific target levels or deadlines for debt reduction. They don’t focus on cutting debt between downturns. And no one independently checks whether these strategies are being met, so they can change from year to year without follow-up.
 The rules we’re proposing have two parts. The first is a long-term debt anchor: a goal for reducing debt over about 10 years. For example, states with higher debt levels might commit to cutting gross debt by 5 percentage points as a share of the economy by 2037.
 That long-term debt anchor would be combined with an annual net spending target, which would cap how much spending can grow each year. It would be set so that states can reach their debt goals even given the variability in their revenue.
 If you overspend the target in one year, you make it up the next year. If you underspend, you can carry that forward. New revenue measures could offset extra spending, and spending cuts could offset tax cuts. There’d also be a separate target for capital spending because, as we’ve discussed, big infrastructure spending has been a major driver of growing debt.
 The trick is to cap what governments choose to spend, not the bottom line. So if a recession hits and revenue falls, the rule doesn’t force cuts, because it’s about spending, not the surplus. And when revenue surprises on the upside, states don’t use that to fund new programs. They use it to pay down debt.
 This model follows recent reforms in places like the European Union, which have set spending caps to give governments at least a 70 per cent chance of hitting their debt anchor. The evidence is really promising. The best evidence from around the world shows strong fiscal rules can reduce deficits by about 0.6 per cent of GDP. That may not sound like a lot, but the combined state fiscal deficit is currently around 1.2 per cent of GDP. So strong fiscal rules in the states could almost halve that deficit.
 To help governments hit those targets, our other recommendation is independent budget offices. Offices like the federal Parliamentary Budget Office play a really important role in budget transparency. By doing budget research and costing policy proposals for parliamentarians, they better inform both parliamentary and public debate.
 An independent budget office can’t replace a government that’s committed to budget repair, but it can definitely help enforce a culture of budget repair.
 The report also has recommendations on getting value for money, particularly in health and infrastructure spending, which go into more depth on how budget processes can better help states repair their budgets.
 Erin-Lea Brown: The way you’ve described the fiscal rules, Matt, strikes a really nice balance. They deal with the actual pressures governments face, they recognise that governments need flexibility, and they acknowledge that without political backing these things don’t work in practice.
 We’re certainly not naive about the challenges fiscal rules present. But by learning from other jurisdictions, we can have another go at implementing them in a way that actually holds governments to account, especially when combined with better institutions that provide transparency.
 So that’s part of the solution when it comes to state budgets and spending. But in the report, we argue that lasting budget repair requires both spending and revenue reform. Can you tell us what we mean by that?
 Matthew Bowes: Fiscal rules help deal with growing government spending, but that’s only half the problem. Spending restraint is clearly essential. Governments need to keep reprioritising, cutting low-value spending, and making sure they’re getting value for money. For the states, that clearly means reviewing a lot of their existing programs.
 But cuts alone can’t close the gap without significantly changing the relationship between the public and government, and Australia’s social bargain.
 For instance, to close the 2024–25 national fiscal deficit through spending cuts alone, governments would have needed cuts about five times larger than the cuts to the NDIS in this year’s federal budget. Anyone following the budget will know those cuts have been very contentious and will be very difficult to achieve. Cutting five times that amount would be a real challenge.
 Part of the spending growth we’ve seen reflects what communities expect from government. Across all advanced economies, government has grown as safety nets have expanded, and as care has moved from unpaid work in the household, particularly work that women do, into publicly funded services like childcare and disability care.
 So any practical plan for repairing budgets needs revenue to be part of the answer, and Australia has room to raise more without being an outlier. Australian governments raise about 29 per cent of GDP in revenue, compared with an average of about 34 per cent across the OECD and comparable advanced economies.
 So we need more revenue, but we also need to make our tax system better, not just bigger. We can’t lean further into damaging taxes, and we shouldn’t rely on bracket creep, which happens when incomes grow and people are pushed into higher personal income tax brackets. We need a tax system that funds services fairly, supports productivity, and makes sense for an ageing population.
 When it comes to revenue, part of the challenge we outline is that states don’t have full control over it. So Erin, why does it matter where the states’ revenue comes from, and how does that affect how they can manage it?
 Erin-Lea Brown: Today, the states spend far more than they raise. They deliver about 42 per cent of total government spending in Australia but raise just 24 per cent of revenue themselves. As a result, federal transfers make up a little under half of state revenue, split roughly evenly between the GST and tied grants.
 That gap between what states spend and what they raise isn’t necessarily a problem. A national government can raise taxes more efficiently, it can stop states undercutting each other on their tax bases, and it can redistribute between states so that Australians get similar services wherever they live. The challenge is managing that gap well, not eliminating it.
 The money states receive in tied grants comes with conditions, and those grants have grown over time. Today there are 200 separate active funding agreements between the federal government and the states, each with its own reporting and conditions.
 And that brings us to the GST. It was meant to be the states’ reliable, growing revenue source, but it’s really not doing that job anymore.
 Matthew Bowes: As you say, Erin, the problem isn’t that the federal government makes transfers to the states. It’s that state budgets are where we need the most immediate repair, and without strong revenue bases to build on, it’s difficult for states to find new revenue to close their deficits and pay down debt.
 Erin-Lea Brown: That’s right, and that’s why in the report we describe this as a national problem that needs a national fix.
 Matthew Bowes: A key part of that national problem centres on the GST. The GST was introduced in 2000 as a consumption tax charged on most goods and services at the checkout, with some notable exemptions such as fresh food, health, and education. It was brought in primarily to give the states a reliable source of revenue. But we argue in this report that it hasn’t kept pace with what’s now being asked of it.
 So why is the GST so important for tax reform?
 Erin-Lea Brown: The GST is a central pillar of how we fund our federation. In 2000, the federal government introduced the GST and gave the states all the revenue, and in return, the states abolished a range of inefficient taxes. That was the last major renegotiation of the federal-state compact.
 Australia makes unusually little use of the GST compared with international peers. It raises about 11 per cent of our total tax revenue, or about 3.3 per cent of GDP, well below the OECD average. At 10 per cent, our rate is among the lowest in the developed world, and it’s covering less of what we buy. Because of the exemptions, the GST covers only about 54 per cent of household spending, down about 7 percentage points since 2000. Spending has shifted towards rent, health, and education, which the GST mostly doesn’t reach.
 Meanwhile, we rely heavily on income tax, and that’s getting harder to sustain. There are about 5.4 working-age Australians for every older Australian today, and that’s projected to fall to 3.4 by 2066. Today, fewer than one in five Australians aged 70 and over pay income tax. Taxing spending rather than earnings reaches people however their spending is funded, whether from wages, super, or savings.
 The GST is also one of our least damaging taxes, and it already goes directly to the states. A bigger, broader GST would give them a stable revenue source that grows with the economy, and potentially room to phase out damaging taxes like stamp duty.
 Matthew Bowes: Every tax reduces economic activity to some extent, and a big part of why the GST should be part of any tax reform discussion is that it’s among the least damaging taxes Australia has.
 The GST doesn’t tax labour or savings. It taxes consumption, and it does that for everyone. That’s really important in an ageing society, because fewer and fewer people will be participating in our income tax system, given the exemptions that apply, particularly to superannuation.
 Erin-Lea Brown: That’s right, Matt. Our report proposes raising the GST to 15 per cent and extending it to all food, which would be a big change at the checkout. Walk us through what we’re proposing. Where does the extra money go, and how would the package make sure low-income households come out ahead?
 Matthew Bowes: It would be a big change at the checkout, but we think there are really good reasons to pursue this kind of major tax reform to help with budget repair.
 We’re proposing to increase the GST rate from 10 per cent to 15 per cent, which would raise about $57 billion a year. We’re also proposing to extend the GST to all food, which raises an additional $19 billion a year. Together, that’s about $76 billion a year in additional revenue. And even at 15 per cent, Australia’s GST rate would still be below the OECD average.
 Taxing all food makes the system a lot simpler. Right now, the GST isn’t applied to things like bacon, frozen chips, and Coco Pops, but it is applied to roasted nuts, some pre-prepared salads, and toothpaste.
 Most of the benefit of these exemptions goes to higher-income households. The poorest 40 per cent of households get only about a third of the benefit of the GST food exemptions. So it’s a poorly targeted way to either improve nutrition or help low-income households, and there are better ways of doing both.
 Instead of spending money on these exemptions, our proposal would expand the GST base and raise the rate, and return a substantial share of the revenue to households through income tax cuts and higher welfare payments.
 We’re proposing about a $33 billion income tax cut – the largest cut to income taxes in about 20 years – along with an increase in welfare payments in the order of $25 billion. That would allow us to increase payments like JobSeeker, Youth Allowance, and Parenting Payment by around 20 per cent, lifting the maximum single rate of JobSeeker by about $80 a week. That addresses a significant gap in our welfare system that many economists and public policy advocates, including Grattan, have been pointing to for years.
 We’re also recommending a 50 per cent increase in Rent Assistance to support low-income renters, and increasing pension rates by about 8 per cent so pensioners don’t go backwards.
 The rest of the revenue can then go towards budget repair. States would end up about $12 billion a year better off, which is enough to almost halve the deficits they’re forecasting over the next couple of years. At the same time, the federal government could save about $6 billion by changing how the GST is distributed, removing the current deal that particularly benefits WA.
 Overall, low-income households would come out ahead. People in the bottom two-fifths of households would receive more in additional welfare support and tax cuts than they pay in extra GST. Higher-income households would pay more, and that’s a deliberate feature of the policy.
 Ultimately, if we need more revenue, people in Australia will have to pay more in tax. But what we get for that is public services that are securely funded for the future, including as our population ages and demand for those services grows. And we get a better deal for future generations, by lowering debt and repairing deficits while the economy is hopefully growing, so that when future crises hit, we have the fiscal space to respond. That’s really important in ensuring future generations get the same economic opportunities previous generations have had.
 Erin-Lea Brown: I think that’s such an important part of our package, Matt. We’ve done the work to identify how the extra GST revenue should actually be spent, in a way that builds trust: the households least able to wear a GST increase won’t be left out of pocket, and in fact will come out ahead.
 That’s been one of the challenges with GST reform in the past. There hasn’t always been a clear articulation of how the money would be used, and how people least able to wear an increase would be supported through the change.
 Matthew Bowes: One more point I’d make is that, over time, our proposal would create additional fiscal space for government. Because of how the income tax cuts and welfare increases are designed, they’ll grow slightly more slowly than the GST revenue we’re forecasting. That gives governments additional room both to repair the deficit and to pursue further rounds of tax and transfer reform. It creates a surer revenue base for the kind of reform that will benefit Australia’s economy in the long run.
 Erin-Lea Brown: That makes sense, and those sorts of changes would be so difficult to make without this kind of revenue reform.
 Matthew Bowes: Exactly.
 Erin-Lea Brown: In the report, we also describe this reform as an opportunity to strike a new federal bargain. What would it take for both levels of government to see themselves as better off, and why is this a deal both sides should say yes to?
 Matthew Bowes: It’s a tricky question, because any attempt to raise taxes will meet a lot of opposition. But we think this is a package that both federal and state governments should see real potential in.
 The starting point is how the GST works today. Since it was introduced, every dollar of GST has gone to the states. That was part of the deal that made the GST possible. But it’s now among the biggest obstacles to reform. If the federal government raises the GST and uses some of the revenue to cut income taxes and boost welfare payments, it carries all the costs of those changes but sees none of the revenue, because under current arrangements it all goes to the states. So any reform package needs a new deal between the two levels of government.
 Erin-Lea Brown: So what you’re saying, Matt, is that we need to give the feds some skin in the game.
 Matthew Bowes: That’s exactly right. We need to give the federal government a reason to want to engage in GST reform, rather than assuming it only benefits the states.
 We propose three changes to make this package work. First, scrapping the GST top-ups from the 2018 WA deal, which would save the federal government about $6 billion a year.
 Second, rebalancing tied federal grants to the states, particularly for things like health and education. We propose reducing them by about $19 billion, mostly by not renewing some agreements as they expire, particularly in areas like infrastructure, where much of this spending already needs to come down at the state level.
 Third, sharing some of the new GST revenue, by giving the federal government 3 percentage points of the new 15 per cent rate, while the states get 12 percentage points on the expanded GST base.
 That would be controversial, because it changes how the GST is distributed. But there are really good reasons for the states to engage in this bargain. They would get $38 billion in untied GST, against a reduction of about $26 billion in the conditional grants they currently receive, leaving them $12 billion better off. As we’ve said, that’s enough to almost halve their forecast deficits over the coming years.
 In the short term, that gives states an opportunity to pay down debt and close deficits. Over time, it would give them room for broader reforms. Because the GST grows with the economy, states would be less exposed to swings in things like house prices and commodity prices, and better placed to handle an ageing population and the cost pressures that come with it.
 It would also give states an opportunity to finally reform revenue bases like stamp duty. Moving from stamp duty to a broad-based land tax is something Grattan and many economists have long recommended. Part of why that reform stalls is that states don’t have other revenue sources to cover the temporary drop in revenue that comes with it, and a bigger GST could help fill that gap.
 But more money for the states isn’t the only answer. States need to sign up to spending discipline and transparency if they’re going to close these deficits. The federal government needs confidence that if it engages in this reform to benefit the states, the states will come to the table with spending restraint of their own. That’s what makes it a bargain: both sides of the federal-state compact coming to the table to make budget repair happen.
 Erin-Lea Brown: And there’s one more reason this matters for the federal government, which you touched on earlier, Matt. The 2018 WA deal on GST distribution costs the federal government billions every year, mostly to ensure that WA – the one state running strong surpluses – can offer better services than all the other states.
 No government wants to be the one that takes money off WA. But a bigger GST pool changes the politics. The impact on WA of changing the distribution system would be far smaller, and every other state would come out ahead. So this reform might actually be the federal government’s only off-ramp from those arrangements.
 Matthew Bowes: That’s exactly right, Erin. There’s an opportunity to reform how GST distribution works so the federal government also benefits, by reducing a costly grant to the states that tops up the GST pool.
 Erin, GST reform has been tried and abandoned before. What’s lost if we leave this reform opportunity on the table?
 Erin-Lea Brown: The first point is that doing nothing isn’t free. It just means the same costs show up later, and bigger.
 Starting with the budget: ageing, climate change, future recessions, and high interest rates are all coming. In our report, we modelled what happens if these hit the budget together over similar timelines. National debt could reach more than three times today’s level by 2066, and state interest bills could eat up nearly a fifth of revenue. That’s money that isn’t going to hospitals or schools.
 Then there’s the tax system. Without reform, we keep relying on bracket creep, taxing a shrinking pool of workers more each year to support a growing number of retirees. The states keep becoming more dependent on the federal government, which will likely mean more tied grants, more time and resources spent on negotiation and compliance, and ultimately a more frustrated federation. And the fight over how the GST is shared isn’t going away. It will only get worse as the pool shrinks relative to the economy.
 We’d also be giving up a lot by not progressing this reform: the biggest income tax cut in nearly 20 years, a JobSeeker payment up by about $80 a week, and a real boost for renters.
 But the biggest loss is choice. Right now, budget repair is something we can choose to do, on our own terms. If we wait, the next crisis may make that choice for us.
 Matthew Bowes: Looking overseas while writing this report, it’s been really clear what happens when debt and deficits spin out of governments’ control. We can see it in France, where there have been large protests against any attempt to cut spending, after a long period in which governments allowed spending to grow without additional revenue. That’s created an imbalance that requires really large adjustments. We have an opportunity now to repair our budgets while, as you say, we still have control over the outcome.
 Erin-Lea Brown: That’s exactly right, Matt. While the recommendations in the report are ones we think should be taken up today, ultimately this report is about the future, and what we can do today to set ourselves up for it.

 Erin-Lea Brown
 Economic Prosperity Deputy Program Director 
 Erin-Lea Brown is a Deputy Program Director in the Grattan Institute’s Economic Prosperity and Democracy Program. Her work focuses on the economy and fiscal policy.
Erin is a former Treasury economist. Before joining Grattan, she was Director of NSW Treasury’s Structural Analysis and Modelling Branch. She has also held roles in the Commonwealth Treasury and the Tasmanian Department of Treasury and Finance. Her experience spans macroeconomic forecasting, economic policy, tax and budget policy, and long-term fiscal sustainability analysis.
Erin holds a First Class Honours degree in International Studies and Arts (Politics/Political Economy) from the University of Wollongong. She also has a Masters of Political Economy from the University of Sydney, where she was awarded the Jo Martins Prize in Political Economy.
